subject: Execution venues, onshore-fallback playbook and cross-border deletion commitments
messages:
From: Elena Rossi <elena@caduceus.health>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Quick Q — where requests are executed and if EU onshore fallback exists

Hi Monica,

Thanks for the demo last week. We have two immediate compliance questions from our security/compliance team as we evaluate Redwood for PII-bearing inference workloads:

1) Where do inference requests from EU users get executed today (region list, high-level subprocessor map)?
2) If EU capacity is constrained, do requests ever transit to the US or other regions? If so, is there an "onshore fallback" (i.e., an option to keep all execution in EU with an on-prem/VPC fallback) or an explicit customer opt-in for cross-border routing?
3) Retention & deletion: how quickly does Redwood propagate user deletion requests through runtime caches, primary stores, and to subprocessors/backups? Please include any standard SLAs.

Can you send a short routing map and a subprocessor inventory (or the locations) we can share with our auditors? If you already have a concise playbook for onshore-fallback behavior that'd be ideal.

Appreciate it — we need this to close our internal gating questions by next week.

Best,
Elena
Security Compliance, Caduceus Health

Subject: Re: Quick Q — where requests are executed and if EU onshore fallback exists

Hi Elena — thanks for the clear list. High level answers below and I'm attaching the execution venue map + current subprocessor inventory. TL;DR: EU traffic is executed in EU by default; cross-border routing only happens under constrained capacity and only with controls (customer opt-in or contract-level routing policy). See details: attachment 'redwood-exec-venues-map.pdf' and 'subprocessor-inventory-2026-09.csv'.

Summary (quick bullets):
- Default execution: requests originating in EU are routed to EU-hosted pools (Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Paris depending on availability).
- Onshore fallback: we offer a configurable routing policy. By default we do NOT route EU production traffic to non-EU regions. Routing fallback to US happens only if a customer enables it in their account settings or signs an escalation DPA addendum that permits cross-border fallback during capacity incidents.
- Temporary transits: transient KV cache shards or telemetry may touch control-plane services in our US control plane, but payloads and model execution remain in-region unless fallback is enabled.
- Deletion: runtime caches are purged within minutes for marked sessions; primary request logs are removed per the DPA timeline (we include standard 30-day deletion windows and longer backup retention — full detail below).

If useful, we can set up a 30-minute walk-through with Rishi and Neha tomorrow to go over the playbook and the technical evidence we can provide for auditors.

Thanks,

Elena / Monica — adding technical detail from infra:

Execution venues and subprocessors (2026-09 snapshot):
- EU compute pools: eu-central-1 (Frankfurt), eu-west-1 (Ireland), eu-west-3 (Paris). These are where model inference runs by default for EU-labeled routes.
- US compute pools: us-west-2 (Oregon), us-east-1 (N. Virginia) used for US-labeled routes and Dedicated pools.
- Subprocessors involved in ephemeral compute orchestration: Cloud provider regional compute & networking teams, managed KMS (customer or Redwood-managed), and a small set of telemetry/log aggregation partners (list attached).

Onshore-fallback behavior and controls:
- Policy-driven routing: each customer can set a route priority. The default template enforces region-pin: EU -> EU only.
- Failover escalation: if EU capacity is fully saturated and the account allows fallback, requests are routed to a pre-authorized fallback pool (usually a nearby US pool) in a hardened encryption enclave. For regulated customers, we require an opt-in signed addendum (DocuSign) before enabling automatic cross-border fallback.
- VPC/Private deployments: for customers who need strict locality, Redwood Private or Dedicated can be provisioned within a customer VPC or dedicated EU zone (no cross-border fallback unless the customer explicitly requests it in writing).

Data lifecycle & deletion propagation:
- Runtime/KV cache: default TTL 24 hours; manual or DPA-triggered deletion results in immediate in-memory eviction and a background tombstone write to the Audit log. Eviction is propagated within seconds to local caches.
- Primary logs/request traces: retained in active stores for up to 30 days by default (customer-configurable). When a deletion request is received (subject to verification), primary records are deleted within our 30-day SLA window; we mark for immediate removal and begin deletion workflow.
- Backups & cold storage: backups are retained up to 90 days (standard) and deleted according to the backup lifecycle policy; we state 90 days in our standard DPA but will negotiate shorter/longer windows as required.
- Subprocessor notices: we push deletion requests to subprocessors via our API contract; subprocessors typically confirm final deletion within 7–30 days depending on their SLA. We provide an evidence pack (audit log entries + confirmation emails) upon request.

Controls & cryptographic protections:
- KMS/HSM: customer-managed KMS keys are supported for encryption-at-rest for customers on Dedicated/Private. For hosted customers, Redwood-managed KMS with HSM-backed keys is available; cross-border fallback still encrypts payloads in transit and at rest.
- Isolation: onshore-fallback pools run in a hardened enclave with restricted egress; we log every fallback and make it available on the customer dashboard and to legal/Security teams via an evidence export.

I'll bring more specifics (subprocessor SLA excerpts, deletion webhook samples, and our evidence checklist) to the call if you want.

—Rishi
VP, Infrastructure — Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Quick Q — where requests are executed and if EU onshore fallback exists

Thanks, Monica and Rishi — helpful. A couple clarifying items from our audit team:

- On backups: can you confirm whether immutable snapshots are ever stored in a different legal jurisdiction from the primary? For example, an EU primary with backups in the US would be a compliance blocker for us.
- On deletion evidence: when you say "we push deletion requests to subprocessors," can you share a sample confirmation artifact (we don't need PII, just the webhook/audit sample and a redacted confirmation from a subprocessor).
- On timescales: we need a maximum end-to-end deletion propagation SLA (including subprocessors) in writing — auditors asked for a single number or range they can rely on. Is 30–60 days a reasonable commitment?

We may request the DPA addendum to prohibit fallback unless Caduceus gives explicit event-by-event approval (i.e., no automatic cross-border fallback). Can you outline how that restriction would be enacted in configuration and what evidence we would get if an operator tried to enable fallback?

Best,
Elena

Elena — answering each of the auditor points below and next steps. See attached 'onshore-fallback-playbook.txt' for exact operator steps and the playbook we would include in the DPA addendum.

1) Backups jurisdiction: by default, backups are kept in the same region family (EU primaries -> EU backups). We do not create cross-region backups in different legal jurisdictions unless explicitly authorized in writing by the customer. We can commit to an EU-only backup placement for Caduceus in the DPA (we'll add the clause).

2) Deletion evidence sample: attached is a redacted audit export template we provide to auditors (includes tombstone record IDs, timestamps, and subprocessor confirmation stubs). For subprocessors that provide async confirmations, we include the confirmation email or webhook receipt as part of the evidence pack. We'll provide a redacted sample in the evidence folder on the drive link.

3) End-to-end SLA: standard candidate commitment we offer is 30–60 days end-to-end (30 days for primary store deletion + up to 30 days for subprocessor/backup confirmation). If Caduceus requires a hard 45-day maximum for all subprocessors, we can negotiate that into the contract for enterprise customers. We'll add explicit verification and reporting obligations for each named subprocessor in the addendum.

4) Prohibiting automatic fallback: we can implement a strict account-level block: account flag 'allow_crossborder_fallback = false' (default for EU-enterprise templates). When set to false, the routing plane will never switch to non-EU pools; any operator action attempting to enable fallback generates an auditable change event requiring a two-person approval and will be logged and surfaced to your security contact. We will provide the UI audit trail and an exported operator approval record.

Next steps:
- I'll upload the redacted evidence sample and the operator playbook to the Drive link in this thread.
- If you'd like the stronger SLA (45-day max) we can have Legal draft that into the DPA addendum — here's a DocuSign link for the addendum draft: https://docusign.example.com/DSEnvelope12345.
- Rishi: will you make sure the subprocessor inventory attached includes the confirmation SLA lines so Elena's auditors can scan them quickly?

Happy to hop on a short call to review the evidence pack.

Thanks,
